PAPER: Journal of Banking Regulation (2026) 27:3 https://doi.org/10.1057/s41261-025-00301-1 ORIGINAL ARTICLE Optimal bank capital: a trade – off corporate finance perspective Federico Beltrame1 Received: 28 July 2025 / Accepted: 11 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract In this paper I model the effect of costs and benefits of having equity on the bank weighted average cost of capital (WACC). Adopting a trade – off corporate finance perspective, costs are related to the loss in present value of debt tax shields and liquidity premium, while benefits are related to the reduction of bank failure probability. The distress effect is incorporated into the bank WACC through the “Cost of leverage” model of Fernandez (2002, 2007), adjusted for the liquidity premium level and for different bank debt policies. Incorporating the cost and benefits on overall cost of bank funding and together with the use of Merton (1974) model, I am able to obtain numerically the optimal level of bank capital, and capital requirements as a whole, for several firm specific and country characteristics (asset volatility, risk-free rate, debt maturity, tax rate, liquidity premium level). A trade off – based framework consistent with traditional corporate finance, presenting results in line with previous literature on bank capital requirements, supports both stability and indi- vidual bank value maximization. JSON: Name: merton_fernandez_bank_capital Title: Estimating optimal bank capital via a structural Merton–Fernandez WACC trade-off framework that endogenizes distress costs and liquidity premia Short Hypothesis: Including endogenous bankruptcy costs and an explicit liquidity premium in a Merton–Fernandez WACC trade-off model causes higher and more predictive optimal Tier 1 capital ratios than models that omit distress-cost endogeneity or liquidity premia. Related Work: Existing approaches to optimal bank capital fall into a few families: (a) regulatory and macro studies that map social-cost estimates of crises into target capital ranges; (b) WACC-based trade-off methods that include tax shields but treat distress costs as exogenous or qualitative; (c) structural credit models (Merton-type) applied to banks for PD estimation; and (d) Fernandez cost-of-leverage formulations for corporate distress costs. Limitations across these strands include: reliance on accounting-based measures or exogenous distress-cost inputs, neglect of a bank-specific liquidity premium embedded in deposit funding, inconsistent treatment of the risk profile of debt benefits (asset-like vs debt-like), limited comparison of alternate debt-policy rules (target debt vs target leverage), and sparse out-of-sample backtests using market signals and supervisory distress events. No prior work jointly calibrates a Merton structural inversion with the Fernandez cost-of-leverage adjusted for bank liquidity premia, and validates the resulting optimal capital estimates against realized bank distress outcomes. Abstract: This project constructs and validates a structural research pipeline to compute bank optimal capital by integrating a Merton structural asset model with a Fernandez cost-of-leverage WACC adjustment that explicitly includes bank liquidity premia and alternative debt-policy rules. The method produces bank-specific optimal equity-to-assets (and translated Tier 1) targets by internalizing bankruptcy costs and the funding advantage of deposits within the WACC. The main contribution is an operational simulation and empirical validation framework: (i) inversion of market equity prices to recover asset value and volatility; (ii) computation of WACC and the present value of distress costs under both target-debt and target-leverage regimes; and (iii) out-of-sample backtests comparing model-implied optimal capital against realized distress events and alternative model baselines. Expected outcomes are: (a) quantification of the incremental impact of distress endogeneity and liquidity premia on optimal capital; (b) evidence that the enriched structural model yields better predictive power for near-term bank distress; and (c) diagnostic scenarios for supervisory stress-testing. Experiments: Datasets: bank-level panel for Euro-area significant and mid-sized banks, 2005–2024, including (i) daily equity prices and implied/realized equity volatility (Bloomberg/Datastream), (ii) bond yields and outstanding debt schedules, (iii) supervisory balance-sheet items and RWA (ECB public supervisory data), (iv) deposit and market funding rates, (v) country-level risk-free yields and corporate tax rates, and (vi) crisis/distress labels (resolution events, supervisory actions, large losses). Synthetic stress scenarios: parameter grids for asset volatility (σa range 2–12%), liquidity premium p (0–50%), risk-free rate (0–5%), debt maturity T (1–10 years). Baselines: (A) WACC trade-off without endogenous distress costs, (B) Fernandez cost-of-leverage excluding liquidity premium, (C) MM vs ME policy variants, (D) accounting-based volatility replacement. Estimation: invert Merton formulas per bank-quarter to recover asset value and σa; compute WACC and optimal E/V via numerical maximization across model variants; Monte Carlo simulation (100,000 paths per scenario) to obtain PD, expected distress costs, and WACC distributions; bootstrap (1,000 resamples) for confidence intervals. Evaluation metrics: predicted optimal Tier 1 ratio, predicted PD (1y and 3y), observed distress within horizon, ROC AUC and Precision-Recall for distress prediction, RMSE between predicted PD and realized binary outcomes (Brier score), mean absolute error between model-implied optimal Tier 1 and observed ex-post supervisory capital shortfall for banks that experienced distress, and Spearman rank correlation of bank risk ordering vs realized outcomes. Ablation studies: remove liquidity premium term; switch debt-benefit risk profile from debt-like to asset-like; fix debt-policy to target-debt vs target-leverage; replace market-derived σa with accounting volatility. Comparisons: statistically test AUC differences (DeLong) and compute economic impact metrics (average reduction in WACC and change in recommended capital under each variant). Out-of-sample protocol: rolling-window estimation with 3-year calibration and 1-year prediction for distress events. Risk Factors and Limitations: Model misspecification: Merton assumptions (log-normal assets, single maturity debt) may not hold for complex bank balance sheets; Fernandez cost-of-leverage closed-form adjustments may not capture all bankruptcy resolution mechanics. Data quality: market prices for small or illiquid banks and subordinated/bail-in debt are noisy; deposit funding and implicit liquidity premia are difficult to observe and may be estimated with measurement error. Endogeneity and simultaneity: market-implied volatility and prices reflect both bank fundamentals and macro shocks, complicating causal interpretation. Cross-jurisdiction heterogeneity: differing accounting rules, tax treatments, and resolution regimes reduce comparability and limit generalization. Event sparsity: realized bank failures/resolutions are rare, limiting statistical power for out-of-sample distress prediction. Computational cost: high-dimension Monte Carlo and bootstrapping across many banks and scenarios requires substantial compute. Policy translation limits: optimal model-implied capital may conflict with regulatory constraints (leverage ratio, TLAC/MREL) and does not capture second-order systemic feedbacks from simultaneous capital adjustments by many banks.
